items.readable_text:
Content:
We have the following formulas that allow us to "factor out" quantifiers to the front of a logical expression:

Content:
[MATH: ∀xP(x)∧Q|≡∀x(P(x)∧Q); ∀xP(x)∨Q|≡∀x(P(x)∨Q); ∃xP(x)∧Q|≡∃x(P(x)∧Q); ∃xP(x)∨Q|≡∃x(P(x)∨Q)]

Content:
In these formulas, note that

Content:
- [MATH: P(x)] is a predicate that depends on [MATH: x] and is within the scope of the quantifier,
- [MATH: Q] is a predicate that does not depend on [MATH: x.]

Content:
Note that both [MATH: P] and [MATH: Q] can include variables other than [MATH: x,] but we've omitted them to simplify these expressions.

Content:
Moving all the quantifiers to the front of a logical expression, we obtain a so-called prenex normal form. Mathematical expressions involving quantifiers are often written in this form.

Content:
For example, let's write the following statement in prenex normal form.

Content:
[MATH: \exists m \in \mathbb{Z} \: (m > 1) \Rightarrow \forall n \in \mathbb{N} \: (10 \mid n)]

Content:
To write this expression in prenex normal form, we need to move all the quantifiers to the front of the expression:

Content:
First, let's introduce the following notation:

Content:
- [MATH: P(m){:} \: m > 1]
- [MATH: Q(n){:} \: 10 \mid n]

Content:
Then, our statement can be written as

Content:
[MATH: \exists m \, P(m) \Rightarrow \forall n \, Q(n).]

Content:
By eliminating the implication, we obtain

Content:
[MATH: ∃mP(m)⇒∀nQ(n)|≡¬(∃mP(m))∨∀nQ(n); ≡∀m¬P(m)∨∀nQ(n).]

Content:
Now, since [MATH: P(m)] does not depend on [MATH: n] and [MATH: Q(n)] does not depend on [MATH: m,] we can move the quantifiers to the front, as follows:

Content:
[MATH: ∀m¬P(m)∨∀nQ(n)|≡∀m(¬P(m)∨∀nQ(n)); ≡∀m∀n(¬P(m)∨Q(n))]

Content:
The final expression gives us a prenex normal form:

Content:
[MATH: \forall m \in \mathbb{Z}, \, \forall n \in \mathbb{N} \, (m \leq 1 \lor 10 \mid n)]

items.readable_text:
Content:
If our predicates depend on the variable used with a quantifier, we have the following two formulas:

Content:
[MATH: ∀xP(x)∧∀xQ(x)|≡∀x(P(x)∧Q(x)); ∃xP(x)∨∃xQ(x)|≡∃x(P(x)∨Q(x))]

Content:
Watch out! What about [MATH: \forall \lor \forall] and [MATH: \exists \land \exists?] It turns out that, in general:

Content:
[MATH: ∀xP(x)∨∀xQ(x)|≢∀x(P(x)∨Q(x)); ∃xP(x)∧∃xQ(x)|≢∃x(P(x)∧Q(x))]

Content:
To see why the [MATH: \forall \lor \forall] case does not hold, consider the following predicates defined over [MATH: \mathbb{Z}{:}]

Content:
- [MATH: P(x){:}] [MATH: x] is odd
- [MATH: Q(x){:}] [MATH: x] is even

Content:
Then, we have

Content:
[MATH: ∀xP(x)∨∀xQ(x)|≡(∀x ∈ Z, [math]x[/math] is odd)∨(∀x ∈ Z, [math]x[/math] is even); = false∨false; = false.]

Content:
Indeed, not all integers are odd, and not all integers are even. Also, the disjunction of two false statements is false.

Content:
On the other hand,

Content:
[MATH: ∀x(P(x)∨Q(x))|≡∀x ∈ Z([math]x[/math] is odd∨[math]x[/math] is even); = true.]

Content:
Indeed, any integer is either even or odd. This statement is true.

Content:
Therefore, [MATH: \forall x \, P(x) \lor \forall x \, Q(x) \not\equiv \forall x \, (P(x) \lor Q(x)).]

Content:
The proof that [MATH: \exists x \, P(x) \land \exists x \, Q(x) \not\equiv \exists x \, (P(x) \land Q(x))] is similar (in fact, we can use the same counterexample).

Content:
Remember that two logical formulas are equivalent if they give the same truth values "for any interpretation," meaning that the left-hand side must be true if and only if the right-hand side is true given any possible predicates and universal sets.

sections.normalized_html:
Recall that two formulas are equivalent if they have the same truth values for all possible concrete predicates.

Let's examine our formulas.

  • We can move the quantifier to the beginning of the formula since the second predicate does not depend on [MATH: x{:}] [MATH: \forall x \, P(x) \land Q \bbox[3pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}\equiv} \forall x \, (P(x) \land Q)]

  • We can move the quantifier to the beginning of the formula since the first predicate does not depend on [MATH: x{:}] [MATH: P \land \forall x \, Q(x) \bbox[3pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}\equiv} \forall x \, (P\land Q(x) )]

  • We can't move a universal quantifier to the beginning of the formula in a disjunction: [MATH: \forall x \, P(x) \lor \forall x \, Q(x) \bbox[3pt,Gainsboro]{\color{red}\not\equiv} \forall x \, (P(x) \lor Q(x))]

[MATH: \qquad] [MATH: \forall x \in \mathbb{R} \, (e^x \gt 0) \Rightarrow \exists y \in \mathbb{R}_{0}^{+} \, (\ln{y} = 1).]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
Let's denote:

  • [MATH: P(x):] [MATH: e^x \gt 0]

  • [MATH: Q(y):] [MATH: \ln{y} = 1]

Then, our statement can be written as [MATH: \forall x \, P(x) \Rightarrow \exists y \, Q(y).]

By eliminating implication, we obtain [MATH: ∀xP(x)⇒∃yQ(y)|≡¬(∀xP(x))∨∃yQ(y); ≡∃x¬P(x)∨∃yQ(y).]

Now, since [MATH: P(x)] does not depend on [MATH: y] and [MATH: Q(y)] does not depend on [MATH: x,] we can move the quantifiers to the front, as follows: [MATH: ∃x¬P(x)∨∃yQ(y)|≡∃x(¬P(x)∨∃yQ(y)); ≡∃x∃y(¬P(x)∨Q(y))]

The final expression reads

[MATH: \qquad] [MATH: \exists x \in \mathbb{R}, \, \exists y \in \mathbb{R}_{0}^{+}, \, (e^{x} \leq 0 \lor \ln{y} = 1).]

We can't "factor out" the quantifier since, in general,

Content:

Content:
However, there is a workaround. If a variable is bound, we can't substitute anything into it. So, we can change any such variables in one of the predicates to some other variable. For example, let's change [MATH: x] to [MATH: y] in the second predicate, as follows:

\equiv \exists x \, P(x) \land \exists \bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}y} \, Q(\bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}y})]

Now, since [MATH: P(x)] does not depend on [MATH: y] and [MATH: Q(y)] does not depend on [MATH: x,] we can move the quantifiers to the front, as follows:

Content:
[MATH: \exists x \, P(x) \land \exists y \, Q(y) \equiv \exists x \, \exists y \, ( P(x) \land Q(y))]

Content:
The final expression reads

[MATH: y]

Content:
So, we get our prenex normal form, but we now have two variables instead of one. Finally, notice that the prenex form is not unique since we could change other occurrences of [MATH: x,] or use [MATH: t] instead of [MATH: y] for the new variable, etc. As a result, we can obtain slightly different resulting expressions.

Then, our statement can be written as

However, we can change the variable in one of the predicates. For example, in the second one:

[MATH: orall x \, P(x) \lor orall x \, Q(x) \equiv orall x \, P(x) \lor orall box[2pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}y} \, Q( box[2pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}y})]

lesson.readable_text:
Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
We have the following formulas that allow us to "factor out" quantifiers to the front of a logical expression:

Content:
[MATH: ∀xP(x)∧Q|≡∀x(P(x)∧Q); ∀xP(x)∨Q|≡∀x(P(x)∨Q); ∃xP(x)∧Q|≡∃x(P(x)∧Q); ∃xP(x)∨Q|≡∃x(P(x)∨Q)]

Content:
In these formulas, note that

Content:
- [MATH: P(x)] is a predicate that depends on [MATH: x] and is within the scope of the quantifier,
- [MATH: Q] is a predicate that does not depend on [MATH: x.]

Content:
Note that both [MATH: P] and [MATH: Q] can include variables other than [MATH: x,] but we've omitted them to simplify these expressions.

Content:
Moving all the quantifiers to the front of a logical expression, we obtain a so-called prenex normal form. Mathematical expressions involving quantifiers are often written in this form.

Content:
For example, let's write the following statement in prenex normal form.

Content:
[MATH: \exists m \in \mathbb{Z} \: (m > 1) \Rightarrow \forall n \in \mathbb{N} \: (10 \mid n)]

Content:
To write this expression in prenex normal form, we need to move all the quantifiers to the front of the expression:

Content:
First, let's introduce the following notation:

Content:
- [MATH: P(m){:} \: m > 1]
- [MATH: Q(n){:} \: 10 \mid n]

Content:
Then, our statement can be written as

Content:
[MATH: \exists m \, P(m) \Rightarrow \forall n \, Q(n).]

Content:
By eliminating the implication, we obtain

Content:
[MATH: ∃mP(m)⇒∀nQ(n)|≡¬(∃mP(m))∨∀nQ(n); ≡∀m¬P(m)∨∀nQ(n).]

Content:
Now, since [MATH: P(m)] does not depend on [MATH: n] and [MATH: Q(n)] does not depend on [MATH: m,] we can move the quantifiers to the front, as follows:

Content:
[MATH: ∀m¬P(m)∨∀nQ(n)|≡∀m(¬P(m)∨∀nQ(n)); ≡∀m∀n(¬P(m)∨Q(n))]

Content:
The final expression gives us a prenex normal form:

Content:
[MATH: \forall m \in \mathbb{Z}, \, \forall n \in \mathbb{N} \, (m \leq 1 \lor 10 \mid n)]

---

Item 2 — Tutorial: When Both Predicates Depend on the Same Variable

Content:
If our predicates depend on the variable used with a quantifier, we have the following two formulas:

Content:
[MATH: ∀xP(x)∧∀xQ(x)|≡∀x(P(x)∧Q(x)); ∃xP(x)∨∃xQ(x)|≡∃x(P(x)∨Q(x))]

Content:
Watch out! What about [MATH: \forall \lor \forall] and [MATH: \exists \land \exists?] It turns out that, in general:

Content:
[MATH: ∀xP(x)∨∀xQ(x)|≢∀x(P(x)∨Q(x)); ∃xP(x)∧∃xQ(x)|≢∃x(P(x)∧Q(x))]

Content:
To see why the [MATH: \forall \lor \forall] case does not hold, consider the following predicates defined over [MATH: \mathbb{Z}{:}]

Content:
- [MATH: P(x){:}] [MATH: x] is odd
- [MATH: Q(x){:}] [MATH: x] is even

Content:
Then, we have

Content:
[MATH: ∀xP(x)∨∀xQ(x)|≡(∀x ∈ Z, [math]x[/math] is odd)∨(∀x ∈ Z, [math]x[/math] is even); = false∨false; = false.]

Content:
Indeed, not all integers are odd, and not all integers are even. Also, the disjunction of two false statements is false.

Content:
On the other hand,

Content:
[MATH: ∀x(P(x)∨Q(x))|≡∀x ∈ Z([math]x[/math] is odd∨[math]x[/math] is even); = true.]

Content:
Indeed, any integer is either even or odd. This statement is true.

Content:
Therefore, [MATH: \forall x \, P(x) \lor \forall x \, Q(x) \not\equiv \forall x \, (P(x) \lor Q(x)).]

Content:
The proof that [MATH: \exists x \, P(x) \land \exists x \, Q(x) \not\equiv \exists x \, (P(x) \land Q(x))] is similar (in fact, we can use the same counterexample).

Content:
Remember that two logical formulas are equivalent if they give the same truth values "for any interpretation," meaning that the left-hand side must be true if and only if the right-hand side is true given any possible predicates and universal sets.

---

Item 3 — Example: Identifying Equivalent Formulas

Example Prompt:
Complete the missing entries in the following statements:

1. [MATH: \forall x \, P(x) \land Q \,\, \bbox[2pt, border: 1pt solid black]{\phantom{AA}}\,\, \forall x \, (P(x) \land Q)]
2. [MATH: P \land \forall x \, Q(x) \,\,\bbox[2pt, border: 1pt solid black]{\phantom{AA}} \,\,\forall x \, (P\land Q(x) )]
3. [MATH: \forall x \, P(x) \lor \forall x \, Q(x) \,\,\bbox[2pt, border: 1pt solid black]{\phantom{AA}} \,\, \forall x \, (P(x) \lor Q(x))]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
Recall that two formulas are equivalent if they have the same truth values for all possible concrete predicates.

Let's examine our formulas.

- We can move the quantifier to the beginning of the formula since the second predicate does not depend on [MATH: x{:}]
[MATH: \forall x \, P(x) \land Q \bbox[3pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}\equiv} \forall x \, (P(x) \land Q)]
- We can move the quantifier to the beginning of the formula since the first predicate does not depend on [MATH: x{:}]
[MATH: P \land \forall x \, Q(x) \bbox[3pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}\equiv} \forall x \, (P\land Q(x) )]
- We can't move a universal quantifier to the beginning of the formula in a disjunction:
[MATH: \forall x \, P(x) \lor \forall x \, Q(x) \bbox[3pt,Gainsboro]{\color{red}\not\equiv} \forall x \, (P(x) \lor Q(x))]

Item 6 — Example: Finding a Prenex Normal Form When the Predicates Have No Common Variables

Example Prompt:
Re-write the following statement by moving all the quantifiers to the front of the expression.

[MATH: \qquad] [MATH: \forall x \in \mathbb{R} \, (e^x \gt 0) \Rightarrow \exists y \in \mathbb{R}_{0}^{+} \, (\ln{y} = 1).]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
Let's denote:

- [MATH: P(x):] [MATH: e^x \gt 0]
- [MATH: Q(y):] [MATH: \ln{y} = 1]

Then, our statement can be written as
[MATH: \forall x \, P(x) \Rightarrow \exists y \, Q(y).]

By eliminating implication, we obtain
[MATH: ∀xP(x)⇒∃yQ(y)|≡¬(∀xP(x))∨∃yQ(y); ≡∃x¬P(x)∨∃yQ(y).]

Now, since [MATH: P(x)] does not depend on [MATH: y] and [MATH: Q(y)] does not depend on [MATH: x,] we can move the quantifiers to the front, as follows:
[MATH: ∃x¬P(x)∨∃yQ(y)|≡∃x(¬P(x)∨∃yQ(y)); ≡∃x∃y(¬P(x)∨Q(y))]

The final expression reads

[MATH: \qquad] [MATH: \exists x \in \mathbb{R}, \, \exists y \in \mathbb{R}_{0}^{+}, \, (e^{x} \leq 0 \lor \ln{y} = 1).]
